newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's General Malan faces judgment day.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's General Malan faces judgment day.

text.p: Former defence minister Magnus Malan, the most senior figure to be tried for atrocities against blacks, faces judgment this week in South Africa's biggest apartheid-era trial.
Malan, 66, and 15 co-defendants face 13 counts of murder for a death squad attack on a black family in KwaMakutha near the east coast city of Durban nine years ago.
He is the most senior member of the country's apartheid government to be charged for abuses committed to maintain white minority rule over the black majority.
Malan, who was head of the country's white-dominated defence force before becoming minister, has repeatedly declared his innocence during the seven-month trial, as have his co-accused.
The judge is expected to start delivering his verdict on Thursday morning.

The state accused him of involvement in setting up a paramilitary force for Mangosuthu Buthelezi's Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party, the main black rivals of Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC).
The massacre of 13 people, six of them children aged from four to 10, was carried out by a death squad allegedly drawn from the Inkatha trainees.
The indictment says Malan was not at the scene of the massacre but was involved in a covert operation that led to it.

The operation included support for Inkatha and Military Intelligence plans to train, arm and finance a team of more than 200 Zulus loyal to the party, to thwart attacks by the then-banned ANC in the mid-1980s.
The prosecution led evidence by an intelligence officer who said he, as liaison officer for the recruits, had planned and ordered the attack on an ANC sympathiser's home.
His junior officer told the court he had ordered the death squad to kill everybody in the house.
Malan has declined to apply for amnesty from South Africa's "truth commission", which is probing 30 years of human rights abuses under apartheid rule.
The state-funded Truth and Reconciliation Commission was set up by President Nelson Mandela's government after it swept to power in the 1994 democracy elections.

The commission can grant amnesty to perpetrators from across the political spectrum if it is convinced the applicant has made a full and honest confession and that the crime was politically motivated.

The commission has begun legal processes to subpoena former police minister Adriaan Vlok, two ex-police generals and six other police chiefs to testify about apartheid-era atrocities committed by the police.
Malan's defence team has argued that although he approved the plan to aid Inkatha he could not have foreseen the trainees would be used to kill supporters of Inkatha's fiercest rivals, the ANC.
Malan is on trial with three generals, a vice-admiral, a senior policeman, two military officers, six Zulus and a top Inkatha official.
Four of the original 20 accused were acquitted earlier in the trial by Judge Jan Hugo because of a lack of evidence against them.

The prosecution has not yet asked for a specific sentence, but legal sources said that if convicted Malan, who faces charges of murder, attempted murder and conspiracy to murder, could face a lengthy jail term.
Hugo will also decide whether to grant three state witnesses indemnity for the role they played in the massacre. Two of the witnesses are ex-officers who admitted to ordering the attack.
